cards.intuition: An encoding understands the type and reshapes values to expose regularity. A codec then treats the encoded result as bytes and squeezes whatever redundancy remains.
cards.formula: typed encoding first, general-purpose byte compression second

cards.intuition: Store each distinct value once and replace every occurrence with a compact dictionary slot number. It is like replacing repeated long names with tiny numbered tickets.
cards.formula: bits per dictionary index = ceiling(log2(distinct values))

cards.intuition: Long consecutive repeats become one value plus a count, while irregular stretches fall back to bit-packed literals. Sorted low-cardinality data gives the hybrid its best case.
If almost every value is distinct, the dictionary grows toward the data itself. Once its capped page overflows, a writer can fall back to plain encoding and file size jumps.
cards.formula: dictionary value falls as distinct count approaches row count

cards.intuition: Compression buys fewer stored and transferred bytes by spending CPU. The right exchange rate depends on whether the query waits for I/O or for decompression.
cards.formula: query time is governed by the active bottleneck: I/O or CPU

cards.intuition: Analytical data is commonly compressed once and read thousands of times. A small write-time saving matters once, while decode cost returns on every scan.
Hot data favors Snappy, LZ4, or low-level Zstd for interactive reads. Cold data can justify stronger Zstd because a one-time compression cost buys long-term storage savings.
cards.formula: hot: fast decode; cold: stronger ratio when amortized

cards.intuition: Postings and Parquet both apply a cheap reversible transform that turns structure into small integers, then encode only the bits those integers need.
cards.formula: structured values → low-entropy residuals → bit packing

cards.intuition: Sorted values make neighboring differences small. Document IDs 1000, 1003, 1007, 1012 become 1000, 3, 4, 5, just as sorted timestamps become compact increments.

cards.concept: Why sortedness pays twice in Parquet
cards.intuition: Nearby values create small deltas and repeated runs for compression, while each row group receives a narrow min-max range for pruning. One write-order choice improves size and reads.
Search scoring needs sequential traversal plus fast skips inside a list. Analytical readers decompress whole pages into vectorized batches, so random access within a page matters less.
cards.formula: postings: traverse and skip; Parquet: decode page and vectorize
